title: Despair to Laughter

source.quote: games such as "Why Don't You—Yes, But,"

setting: Thursday, coffee after work. Theo has a problem with his landlord again - the fourth version of some unsolvable problem this month - and he's doing the thing he always does.

L1.line: Why don't you just - no, wait, I already thought of that, it won't work either.
cues: rejects the suggestion before it's even offered
the ask-then-reject rhythm repeats every time
L1.question: What is Theo actually asking for here, and from which ego state?

options.text: He's asking from Adult, gathering information to solve a real problem.
options.feedback: A genuine Adult request would wait to hear an answer before deciding it won't work. Rejecting the suggestion before it even exists isn't information-gathering.

options.text: He's asking from Child, running "Why Don't You - Yes, But" - the point isn't the advice, it's proving nobody can actually help.
options.feedback: Right. The game's payoff is the proof that help doesn't work, not the help itself - every offered answer just needs to be shot down, which is why the suggestions never actually land.

options.text: He's asking from Parent, testing whether you'll follow his standards.
options.feedback: He's not imposing a rule on you here - he's soliciting rescue, not judging your compliance with some standard.

L1.lesson: "Why Don't You - Yes, But" is played from Child, soliciting a stream of Parent-flavored advice only to reject each piece - the antithesis isn't a better suggestion, it's refusing to supply suggestions at all.

L2.intro: Jordan has watched Theo do this with five different friends this month. Time to hold the antithesis instead of playing along - however many rounds it takes.

beats.line: I don't know what to do about my landlord, he's completely impossible.

options.outcome: "I mean... nothing yet. I just want someone to tell me what to do."
options.lesson: Handing the question back instead of supplying an answer is the antithesis to "Why Don't You - Yes, But": the game only runs if someone keeps offering suggestions to reject.

options.outcome: "It is! You have no idea." Sympathetic, but the opening isn't challenged either way.
options.lesson: Naming the feeling keeps Jordan out of the Rescuer seat for now, which is fine once - but it doesn't move anything, since no advice has been offered yet for Theo to reject.

options.text: Why don't you just send him a formal written notice about it?
options.outcome: "Yeah, but he doesn't even read his mail." First Yes-But, right on cue.
options.lesson: Taking the bait is exactly the Rescuer move the game is built to invite - and because this is a game-move, the exchange ends right here, before it can go any further.

beats.line: Come on, you always have good ideas - what would YOU actually do?

options.text: I think you already know what you'd do if you weren't scared of the fight.
options.outcome: Theo goes quiet. "...Maybe I do, actually."
options.lesson: The antithesis has to survive the second push, not just the first ask - escalation is the game testing whether the refusal was real or just polite.

options.text: I really don't know your landlord or your lease well enough to say.
options.outcome: "Ugh, fine." True, and a little cold - he backs off but looks stung.
options.lesson: This dodges the bait without landing anywhere - a defensible non-answer, but it doesn't open the door the way handing the question back does.

options.text: Okay, fine - I'd call a tenants' rights hotline.
options.outcome: "Yeah, but I tried calling one of those once and it just rang forever." Second Yes-But.
options.lesson: Caving on the second round is the classic trap: persistence of the Rescuer, not any one offer, is what keeps these games running indefinitely.

beats.line: Wow. I thought you actually cared about this. I guess not.
cues: testing whether Jordan will fold to avoid the accusation

options.text: I do care - that's exactly why I'm not going to hand you an answer you'll just shoot down.
options.outcome: Silence. Then: "...Oh my god. I do that, don't I?"
options.lesson: Naming the pattern out loud is itself a strong antithesis - the move doesn't have to be a refusal, it can be the insight that breaks the frame.

options.text: Sorry, I didn't mean it like that.
options.outcome: "Good. So what should I do?" Straight back to square one.
options.lesson: Apologizing under the guilt-trip slides Jordan into Adapted Child and reopens the exact door the antithesis had just closed.

options.text: Fine, fine - maybe take a video of the leak and send it to the housing board.
options.outcome: "Yeah, but I don't even have a decent camera." Third Yes-But.
options.lesson: Same move, third time - the game can run as many rounds as the Rescuer keeps supplying material for.

beats.line: ...I ask people for advice and then explain why it won't work. I've done this with like five different friends this month, haven't I?

options.text: Yeah. You just did it about three times in the last five minutes, with me.
options.outcome: Theo bursts out laughing. "Oh my god - there I go again!"
options.lesson: This is the marker Berne and Steiner point to: despair tipping into real laughter is what it looks like when someone sees their own pattern from Adult, not just hears it described.

options.text: It's okay, honestly, we all do stuff like this.
options.outcome: Theo nods, half-smiles - the laugh doesn't quite land, the moment passes.
options.lesson: Comforting dampens the Aha! right when it's arriving - useful earlier in the conversation, but here it takes the heat off before the pattern can be fully felt.

options.text: Do you want help making a list of what hasn't worked so far?
options.outcome: "Yes! Let's start with the landlord thing." Right back into round one.
options.lesson: Offering to help organize the problem is a Rescue wearing a helpful mask - it restarts the whole loop one line before the finish.

fields.label: In under 50 words: what is "antithesis" in Berne's sense, and why did holding it here take three rounds instead of one?

echo.setting: Five days later, a group chat message from Theo about a different unsolvable problem, same rhythm.
echo.line: "Okay don't even suggest X, I already know it won't work, but what do you think I should do??"
